messages.subject: Re: information on platform design
parts:
Nino-

I suggest that you read section 6.10 of the Advanced Distance Sampling
book if you have not already done so. While it does not completely
answer your question it does address some issues that you are asking
about. The answer to your questions depends on the species and what you
are trying to accomplish. I presume that what you are trying to do is
use the secondary observer to set up trial detections for the primary
observer to estimate detection probability that is unaffected by
potential movement of cetaceans and to assess availability bias. The
answer of how "high" for the secondary observer depends on how far away
you can see the cetaceans, how far away you expect that they may respond
(if at all) to the vessel and what their average dive times are. For
movement you want the secondary observer to detect them before they
respond and for availability bias(diving) you want the time between
possible detections of primary and secondary to exceed the length of the
average dive interval.

"which ones could be the benefits/disavantages in not keeping to or
observing it?"
I'm not certain what you mean by the above. If you are asking is it
worth doing a secondary observer, that will again depend on the species
you are surveying and how likely responsive movement will occur and
whether detection probability will be close to 1.

Much of this is species specific. I suggest that you do a thorough
literature search for papers about surveys and survey techniques for the
species you are interested in.

regards --jeff laake
